    It seems appropriate in this chapter merely to list the members of the faculty with their respective teaching fields as an indication of the growth of the College and to describe the education of each, wherever it is known, as a measure of the quality and character of the standards of the school. More extended thumbnail sketches of these teachers are reserved for treatment in Chapter VI, for the purposes therein explained.

    President Halsell was the only teacher to remain with the College for all of its years. His training in the Lawyer's skill, to be dealt with in his further personal study, gave him a special background in argumentation and oratory. In his early College he was responsible particularly for the Latin and Rhetoric, though in the earlier years he carried his share of Preparatory classes, and in the intermediate years taught Latin. A broad and versatile man, he seems to have, after a period at Savoy College, studied medicine in the Medical College at Louisville, and returned to Fannin County to the practice of the medical profession.

    The Reverend Mr. Holland was of the longest in period of service, served ten years after his first connection with the school early in 1883 to about 1893. He was actually Professor of Greek, Latin, and Mental and Moral Science. From his foundation training in the Glenville, West Virginia Institute he developed a versatility on which continued with him throughout his teaching career. In addition to this training, which suggested a superior standard, his standing in the classical languages was the hallmark of the College's classical standard—Greek was clearly his chosen worship, and his immediate successor in the chair of Greek was one of his own students who had received the A.B. degree of the College.
